triage.name: Edema
triage.reason: A common symptom with a broad cardiorenal-hepatic differential that students evaluate through history, exam and labs.

demographics: More common with increasing age as heart, kidney and venous disease accumulate
Leg swelling from chronic venous disease is more common in women
Pitting leg edema in pregnancy is common in the third trimester

risk_factors.text: Chronic kidney disease or nephrotic syndrome
Chronic venous insufficiency or prior deep vein thrombosis
Lymphedema after lymph node surgery or radiation
Prolonged standing or walking in hot weather

comorbidities: Prior cancer treatment with lymph node dissection or radiation
social_history: Limited mobility or long periods of sitting

chief_complaints.text: My legs and ankles are swollen
My shoes feel tight by the end of the day
I've gained weight and my whole body feels puffy

hpi.onset: Gradual over days to weeks; sometimes noticed after a period of standing or a salty meal
hpi.duration: Usually weeks to months by the time it is evaluated
hpi.progression: Slowly worsens through the day and over weeks; may improve overnight and with leg elevation
hpi.location: Both lower legs and ankles, often symmetric; can involve the hands, face, abdomen or whole body depending on the cause
hpi.quality: Puffy, doughy fullness of the skin that leaves a dent when pressed
hpi.severity: Mild to moderate; tightness and heaviness rather than pain
hpi.timing: Worse in the evening and after standing; better after a night in bed or with legs raised
aggravating: Standing or sitting for long periods

associated_symptoms.text: Weight gain over the same period
Waking up short of breath at night

pertinent_negatives: Recent long travel or immobility with one-sided swelling
Known cancer with new focal swelling

positives.text: Swelling of both ankles and legs
Needing extra pillows to breathe at night

argues_against: One-sided calf pain and swelling suggesting deep vein thrombosis

positives.text: Waking at night short of breath

argues_against: Sudden severe shortness of breath with chest pain
Hematemesis or melena pointing to variceal bleeding
Dysuria and fever suggesting urinary infection

positives.text: Skin feels tight and shiny over the swollen area

negatives: Redness or warmth of the leg
argues_against: Cellulitis or stasis ulcer with infection
Systemic illness with fever and weight loss

atypical.how_it_differs: Swelling may be attributed to aging or arthritis; heart failure and kidney disease are more likely and medications contribute more often.
missing_classic_features: Clear temporal pattern of evening worsening

atypical.how_it_differs: Mild symmetric leg swelling is expected in the third trimester; new facial or hand swelling with headache or visual changes suggests preeclampsia and needs urgent evaluation.
Edema is often generalized with facial and periorbital puffiness, foamy urine and reduced urine output rather than isolated leg swelling.
Swelling comes with abdominal distension from ascites, easy bruising and jaundice rather than pure leg edema.
missing_classic_features: Legs as the only swollen area

atypical.how_it_differs: Edema is more often from nephrotic syndrome or allergic reactions; periorbital swelling in the morning is a common clue.

general.mild: Comfortable, well-appearing; swelling noticed mainly by tight shoes or socks
general.moderate: Well-appearing but uncomfortable; legs feel heavy and tight by evening
general.severe: Ill-appearing with tense, shiny skin; may be short of breath on minimal exertion
general.critical: Toxic or lethargic; respiratory distress at rest, anasarca, or an infected/ulcerated leg

findings.maneuver: Press a fingertip firmly over the dorsum of the foot or the medial malleolus for several seconds, then release
findings.finding: A persistent dent (pitting) that slowly refills

findings.maneuver: Compare both lower legs and ankles side by side
findings.finding: Symmetric bilateral swelling

findings.maneuver: Inspect the feet, ankles and legs with the patient seated or standing
findings.finding: Swelling is greatest in the most dependent areas and improves with elevation

findings.maneuver: Inspect the skin over the swollen legs
findings.finding: Skin is stretched, shiny and taut

findings.maneuver: Inspect the lower legs for indentations from socks or shoes
findings.finding: Deep sock or shoe marks

findings.maneuver: Inspect the lower legs for brown discoloration, varicosities or ulcers
findings.finding: Hemosiderin staining, varicose veins or a medial malleolar ulcer suggesting chronic venous disease

findings.maneuver: Inspect the internal jugular vein with the patient at 30–45 degrees
findings.finding: Elevated jugular venous pressure

findings.maneuver: Auscultate the heart at the apex with the bell
findings.finding: Third heart sound (S3 gallop)
Bibasilar crackles

findings.maneuver: Percuss the flanks and test for shifting dullness
findings.finding: Ascites with abdominal distension

findings.maneuver: Inspect the face and around the eyes in the morning
findings.finding: Periorbital or facial puffiness suggesting renal causes

findings.maneuver: Compare calf size and palpate the calf on the more swollen side
findings.finding: One-sided calf swelling and tenderness suggesting deep vein thrombosis

findings.maneuver: Palpate the calf and check for warmth and erythema
findings.finding: Unilateral warmth, redness and tenderness suggesting cellulitis or DVT

findings.maneuver: Press firmly over the swollen area and observe whether a dent remains
findings.finding: Firm, non-pitting swelling suggesting lymphedema or myxedema

findings.maneuver: Palpate the knees and ankles for warmth, effusion and synovitis
findings.finding: No joint effusion or synovitis
Clear lungs without crackles or wheeze

labs.caveat: A low value makes heart failure unlikely as the cause of the swelling; higher values track with worse heart failure but are also raised in kidney disease and with age.
Interpret with age and kidney function; values rise as GFR falls.
A rising creatinine points to a renal cause or to over-diuresis; a normal value does not exclude nephrotic syndrome.
Rises with reduced kidney perfusion, heart failure and diuresis.
Low albumin suggests nephrotic syndrome, cirrhosis or protein-losing states and lowers the effective response to diuretics.
Raised in hepatic causes of edema and ascites.
Thrombocytopenia with edema suggests cirrhosis with portal hypertension.
Prolonged in hepatic synthetic dysfunction; also raised by warfarin.
Hyponatremia is common in heart failure, cirrhosis and over-diuresis; it limits how aggressively diuretics can be pushed.
Loop and thiazide diuretics cause hypokalemia; kidney disease and potassium-sparing diuretics cause hyperkalemia.
Diabetes is a common driver of kidney disease and edema.
Severe hypothyroidism causes non-pitting myxedema; it is a treatable cause of swelling.
Protein on dipstick points to a renal cause; quantify with a urine protein-to-creatinine ratio.
Blood with protein suggests glomerulonephritis rather than nephrotic syndrome.
RBC casts are specific for glomerulonephritis.
Anemia with edema suggests chronic kidney disease or cirrhosis.
Ordered when edema comes with chest pain or acute decompensated heart failure; a rise suggests an acute coronary syndrome or demand ischemia.

Negative. Required in anyone who could be pregnant before imaging and before starting diuretics or renin-angiotensin blockade; new swelling with headache or visual change in pregnancy suggests preeclampsia.

findings.finding: Atrial fibrillation
Sinus tachycardia
Low voltage in the limb leads
Left ventricular hypertrophy with repolarization changes
Diffuse ST depression and T-wave flattening suggesting strain
Electrical alternans with low voltage suggesting a large pericardial effusion

findings.text: Reduced left ventricular ejection fraction with dilated chambers
Left ventricular hypertrophy with preserved or mildly reduced ejection fraction
Moderate or greater diastolic dysfunction
Dilated inferior vena cava that does not collapse with inspiration
Moderate or larger pericardial effusion
Severe tricuspid regurgitation with right ventricular dilation suggesting right heart failure
Normal study
Cardiomegaly
Pulmonary vascular congestion or interstitial edema
Bilateral pleural effusions
Normal heart size and clear lungs

imaging.study: Ultrasound of the lower extremity veins with compression
imaging.preferred_when: Unilateral or asymmetric leg swelling, or calf pain and warmth

findings.text: Noncompressible deep vein with echogenic thrombus
Absent or reduced phasic flow in the deep veins with Valsalva
No deep vein thrombus identified

imaging.study: Ultrasound of the abdomen with Doppler of the portal and hepatic veins

findings.text: Coarse echogenic liver with nodular contour suggesting cirrhosis
Ascites
Splenomegaly
Reversed or reduced portal venous flow
Small, echogenic kidneys suggesting chronic kidney disease

imaging.study: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
imaging.preferred_when: When cirrhosis, portal vein thrombosis or malignancy is suspected and ultrasound is inconclusive

findings.text: Nodular liver with ascites and varices
Portal or splenic vein thrombosis
Bilateral enlarged kidneys suggesting nephrotic syndrome
Enlarged echogenic kidneys suggesting nephrotic syndrome
Small echogenic kidneys suggesting chronic kidney disease
Hydronephrosis

initial.why: Anemia, thrombocytopenia or leukocytosis point to kidney disease, cirrhosis or infection
Assesses kidney function, sodium and potassium before and during diuresis
Albumin, bilirubin and transaminases screen for hepatic and nephrotic causes
Protein, blood and casts separate renal causes from cardiac and venous ones
Supports or argues against heart failure as the cause of the swelling
Hypothyroidism is a treatable cause of non-pitting edema
Rules out pregnancy before imaging and before starting diuretics or renin-angiotensin blockade
Defines cardiac structure and function when heart failure is suspected
Looks for cardiomegaly, congestion and pleural effusions
initial.only_if: dyspnea, orthopnea or crackles are present

initial.test: Ultrasound of the lower extremity veins with compression
initial.only_if: swelling is unilateral or asymmetric, or the calf is painful and warm

confirmatory.why: Quantifies proteinuria and confirms nephrotic-range protein loss when the dipstick is positive

supporting.why: Alternative natriuretic peptide when BNP is unavailable
Looks for myocardial injury when edema comes with chest pain or acute decompensation
Supports an inflammatory or infectious process such as cellulitis

supporting.test: Ultrasound of the abdomen with Doppler of the portal and hepatic veins
supporting.only_if: ascites, thrombocytopenia or abnormal liver tests are present
proteinuria or reduced kidney function is found

not_indicated.why: Low specificity in edema; a negative result may help only when DVT is unlikely and imaging is not readily available

not_indicated.test: ct abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
not_indicated.why: Not a routine test for edema; reserved for suspected portal vein thrombosis or malignancy
not_indicated.only_if: cirrhosis or malignancy is suspected and ultrasound is inconclusive

not_indicated.why: No role unless abdominal pain suggests pancreatitis
Not needed unless there is respiratory distress or a suspected acid-base disorder
Not needed unless infection such as cellulitis is suspected

decision_points: Decide first whether the swelling is localized or generalized: unilateral swelling needs venous ultrasound, generalized swelling needs a cardiac, renal and hepatic workup
Check a pregnancy test before imaging and before starting diuretics or renin-angiotensin blockade in anyone who could be pregnant
A low BNP makes heart failure unlikely; a high BNP can also come from kidney disease, so interpret with creatinine and age
Dipstick protein should be quantified with a urine protein-to-creatinine ratio before labeling nephrotic syndrome
Weigh the patient daily during diuresis; a rapid creatinine rise or hypotension means the diuretic dose is too high

differential.name: Deep vein thrombosis
differential.why_considered: Unilateral or asymmetric leg swelling is the classic presentation and can be mistaken for dependent edema
differential.trigger: Swelling that is unilateral, asymmetric, or accompanied by calf pain, warmth or recent immobility

history: Recent surgery, hospitalization, long travel or immobilization
Active cancer or prior VTE
Calf pain or tightness on the affected side
exam: Calf circumference difference of 3 cm or more
Unilateral warmth, erythema and tenderness along the deep veins
labs: D-dimer negative makes DVT unlikely in low-risk patients
imaging: Noncompressible deep vein with echogenic thrombus on compression ultrasound

differential.name: Cellulitis
differential.why_considered: A swollen, red, warm leg can look like edema with skin changes
differential.trigger: Fever, rapidly spreading erythema, or focal pain out of proportion to the swelling

history: Fever and chills
Rapid onset over hours to a day
Skin break, insect bite or prior episode
exam: Unilateral, sharply demarcated erythema with warmth and tenderness
Lymphangitic streaking or regional lymphadenopathy

differential.name: Heart failure
differential.why_considered: The most common systemic cause of bilateral pitting leg edema

history: Exertional dyspnea, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea
Rapid weight gain over days
exam: Elevated jugular venous pressure
S3 gallop, bibasilar crackles
Edema improves overnight with elevation
imaging: Reduced ejection fraction or diastolic dysfunction on echocardiogram
Cardiomegaly and pulmonary congestion on chest x-ray

differential.name: Nephrotic syndrome
differential.why_considered: Generalized edema with periorbital and facial puffiness, especially in younger patients

history: Foamy urine
Recent weight gain and generalized swelling
Periorbital puffiness worse in the morning
exam: Periorbital or facial edema
Anasarca in severe cases
labs: Urine protein-to-creatinine ratio in the nephrotic range
imaging: Enlarged echogenic kidneys on renal ultrasound

differential.name: Cirrhosis with portal hypertension
differential.why_considered: Ascites and peripheral edema from low albumin and portal hypertension

history: Heavy alcohol use or chronic hepatitis
Abdominal distension, easy bruising
Jaundice
exam: Ascites with shifting dullness
Spider angiomata, palmar erythema, caput medusae
Splenomegaly
imaging: Coarse nodular liver with ascites and splenomegaly on ultrasound

differential.name: Chronic venous insufficiency
differential.why_considered: Long-standing bilateral leg swelling that worsens through the day and improves with elevation

history: Years of swelling worse in the evening and in warm weather
Improves with leg elevation and compression
Often worse after prolonged standing
exam: Hemosiderin staining, varicose veins, medial malleolar ulcers
Pitting edema without tenderness or warmth
imaging: Venous reflux or obstruction on duplex ultrasound

differential.name: Lymphedema
differential.why_considered: Non-pitting, firm swelling that does not improve overnight

history: Prior lymph node dissection, radiation or recurrent cellulitis
Swelling is progressive and does not improve with elevation or diuretics
exam: Non-pitting, firm, thickened skin
Positive Stemmer sign (unable to pinch the dorsal skin fold of the toe)

differential.name: Hypothyroidism with myxedema
differential.why_considered: Non-pitting edema with fatigue and weight gain

history: Cold intolerance, constipation, dry skin, hair loss
Weight gain despite poor appetite
exam: Non-pitting, doughy swelling of the face, hands and legs
Delayed relaxation of deep tendon reflexes
Bradycardia
labs: Elevated TSH with low free T4

differential.name: Medication-related edema
differential.why_considered: Common cause of bilateral dependent edema with no other systemic findings

history: Started amlodipine, nifedipine, gabapentin, pregabalin, pioglitazone or a NSAID weeks before the swelling
Swelling improves when the drug is stopped
exam: Bilateral pitting edema without jugular venous distension, crackles or ascites

severity.mild: Swelling noticed mainly by tight shoes or socks; no dyspnea, no weight change, normal vitals and oxygen saturation
severity.moderate: Visible bilateral pitting edema with heaviness and evening worsening; mild exertional dyspnea or modest weight gain; may have elevated jugular venous pressure or crackles
severity.severe: Tense, shiny legs with marked pitting, orthopnea, dyspnea on minimal exertion, ascites or anasarca; hypoxemia or hypotension may be present
severity.critical: Respiratory distress at rest, anasarca with hemodynamic compromise, or an infected or ulcerated leg with sepsis; also flash pulmonary edema or cardiogenic shock

red_flags.finding: Unilateral leg swelling with calf pain or warmth
red_flags.meaning: Deep vein thrombosis until proven otherwise; needs compression ultrasound

red_flags.finding: Fever, spreading erythema or focal tenderness
red_flags.meaning: Cellulitis or necrotizing infection; needs urgent antibiotics and possibly surgical evaluation

red_flags.finding: Dyspnea at rest, orthopnea or new hypoxemia
red_flags.meaning: Acute decompensated heart failure or pulmonary edema; needs urgent treatment

red_flags.finding: Rapid weight gain over days with worsening edema
red_flags.meaning: Volume overload from heart failure or renal disease; diuresis may be needed

red_flags.finding: New facial or hand swelling with headache or visual changes in pregnancy
red_flags.meaning: Preeclampsia; needs urgent blood pressure and laboratory evaluation
Cardiogenic shock, sepsis or over-diuresis; reassess volume status and diuretic dose

special_populations.differences: Heart failure, kidney disease and medication effects are more common; swelling may be attributed to aging or arthritis, and diuresis must be cautious because of reduced renal reserve.

Mild symmetric leg swelling is expected in the third trimester; new facial or hand swelling with headache or visual changes suggests preeclampsia and needs urgent evaluation. Avoid diuretics and renin-angiotensin blockade.
Edema is often generalized with periorbital puffiness, foamy urine and reduced urine output; diuretic response is blunted by low albumin and reduced GFR, and electrolytes need close monitoring.
Swelling comes with ascites, easy bruising and jaundice; albumin is low, INR is prolonged and thrombocytopenia is common. Avoid NSAIDs and large-volume paracentesis without albumin.
Edema is more often from nephrotic syndrome or allergic reactions; periorbital swelling in the morning is a common clue and blood pressure should be checked.
Swelling may be attributed to weight alone; obesity-related lymphedema and venous insufficiency are common, and BNP interpretation is less reliable.

key_questions.question: Is the swelling in one leg or both?
key_questions.looking_for: Bilateral and symmetric suggests a systemic cause; unilateral or asymmetric raises concern for deep vein thrombosis or cellulitis

key_questions.question: When did it start, and has it been getting worse?
key_questions.looking_for: Gradual over days to weeks suggests a systemic cause; sudden onset over hours suggests thrombosis or infection

key_questions.question: Is it worse at the end of the day and better after a night in bed with your legs up?
key_questions.looking_for: Evening worsening that improves with elevation fits dependent edema from heart, kidney or venous disease

key_questions.question: Does pressing on the swollen area leave a dent?
key_questions.looking_for: Pitting suggests cardiac, renal, hepatic or venous causes; firm non-pitting swelling suggests lymphedema or myxedema

key_questions.question: Where else are you swollen — face, hands, belly?
key_questions.looking_for: Periorbital or facial puffiness suggests a renal cause; abdominal distension suggests ascites from cirrhosis or heart failure

key_questions.question: Have you gained weight recently, and over how long?
key_questions.looking_for: Rapid weight gain over days suggests volume overload from heart failure or renal disease

key_questions.question: Are you short of breath with activity, or do you wake up short of breath at night?
key_questions.looking_for: Exertional dyspnea, orthopnea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea point to heart failure

key_questions.question: Do you need more pillows to sleep comfortably?
key_questions.looking_for: Orthopnea suggests pulmonary congestion from heart failure

key_questions.question: Is your urine foamy, bloody or reduced in amount?
key_questions.looking_for: Foamy urine suggests proteinuria; blood suggests glomerulonephritis; reduced output suggests kidney failure

key_questions.question: Do your legs feel painful, warm or red on one side?
key_questions.looking_for: Unilateral pain, warmth and redness suggest deep vein thrombosis or cellulitis and need urgent evaluation

key_questions.question: Any fever or chills?
key_questions.looking_for: Fever with a swollen red leg suggests cellulitis or another infection

key_questions.question: Have you had recent surgery, a hospitalization, long travel, or been off your feet?
key_questions.looking_for: Recent immobility or surgery raises the risk of deep vein thrombosis

key_questions.question: Have you been told you have heart failure, kidney disease or liver problems?
key_questions.looking_for: Established cardiac, renal or hepatic disease makes that cause much more likely

key_questions.question: Have you had cancer treatment, lymph node surgery or radiation?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior lymph node dissection or radiation suggests lymphedema

key_questions.question: What medications do you take, including anything new in the last few weeks?
key_questions.looking_for: Amlodipine, nifedipine, gabapentin, pregabalin, pioglitazone, prednisone or NSAIDs can cause edema

key_questions.question: Do you take water pills, and have you missed any doses?
key_questions.looking_for: Missed diuretics explain worsening swelling; over-diuresis explains hypotension and rising creatinine

key_questions.question: How much salt do you eat, and do you add salt at the table?
key_questions.looking_for: High sodium intake worsens edema and blunts diuretic response

key_questions.question: Do you stand or sit for long periods at work?
key_questions.looking_for: Prolonged standing supports dependent or venous edema

key_questions.question: Could you be pregnant? When was your last period?
key_questions.looking_for: Pregnancy changes the workup; new facial or hand swelling with headache or visual changes suggests preeclampsia

key_questions.question: Any chest pain, palpitations or fainting?
key_questions.looking_for: Cardiac symptoms raise concern for heart failure or an acute coronary syndrome

key_questions.question: Any vomiting blood, black stools or yellowing of the eyes or skin?
key_questions.looking_for: Suggests cirrhosis with portal hypertension and varices

key_questions.question: Any joint swelling or morning stiffness?
key_questions.looking_for: Joint involvement suggests an inflammatory arthritis rather than edema

key_questions.question: Any cold intolerance, constipation or dry skin?
key_questions.looking_for: Hypothyroidism is a treatable cause of non-pitting edema

reasoning_points: Bilateral symmetric pitting edema that worsens through the day and improves with elevation
Distribution and associated symptoms point to a cardiac, renal, hepatic or venous cause rather than a local one
Exertional dyspnea, orthopnea or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea with elevated jugular venous pressure or crackles supports heart failure
Foamy urine, periorbital puffiness or reduced urine output with proteinuria and low albumin supports a renal cause
Ascites, thrombocytopenia, low albumin and prolonged INR support cirrhosis with portal hypertension
A new medication such as amlodipine, gabapentin or an NSAID is a common and reversible cause
Unilateral swelling with calf pain or warmth must be evaluated for deep vein thrombosis or cellulitis before assuming systemic edema
Pregnancy must be excluded before imaging and before starting diuretics or renin-angiotensin blockade
A low BNP makes heart failure unlikely, while a high BNP can also come from kidney disease and must be interpreted with creatinine and age

easy: Older adult with known heart failure and classic evening-worsening bilateral pitting leg edema
Orthopnea, elevated jugular venous pressure, bibasilar crackles and an elevated BNP
medium: New amlodipine started weeks before the swelling, with a normal cardiac, renal and hepatic workup
Nephrotic syndrome with periorbital puffiness, foamy urine and low albumin
Cirrhosis with ascites, thrombocytopenia and prolonged INR
Chronic venous insufficiency with years of evening swelling, hemosiderin staining and varicose veins
hard: Unilateral leg swelling with calf pain in a patient who also has chronic bilateral edema
Non-pitting firm swelling after lymph node dissection that does not improve with elevation or diuretics
Hypothyroidism with doughy non-pitting swelling, fatigue and weight gain
Pregnant patient with new facial and hand swelling and headache suggesting preeclampsia
Older adult on multiple medications with edema attributed to aging, where a drug cause is the real explanation
